title: 論語 里仁第四
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 4, 〈里仁〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 4 of the Analects, 里仁 Lǐ rén, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In a village, humaneness…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost every passage in this book is a single short saying of the Master. The first seven all turn on humaneness (仁 rén), the virtue the whole Analects circles: who has it, how rarely it is loved, and how it shows even in a man's faults (4.1–4.7). Then come sayings on the Way and what is right against profit (4.8–4.17), among them the famous exchange in which Confucius tells Master Zeng that one thing runs through his whole Way, and Master Zeng explains it to the others as wholeheartedness and fellow-feeling (4.15); then a group on serving one's parents (4.18–4.21), and short sayings on being slow to speak (4.22–4.24). Each numbered passage (4.1–4.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 4.14 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
里仁為美。
擇不處仁，
焉得知？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “In a village, humaneness is the beauty.
Choosing, and not settling among humaneness —
how can that be wise?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What makes a neighbourhood fine is the humaneness of the people in it. A man who picks where to live and passes over a place where humaneness is — what wisdom is there in that?”
sentences.n: The book is named 里仁 from its first words. Nearly all of its 26 passages are short sayings of the Master, and the first seven all turn on 仁, humaneness. 里 is a village or ward, the place where people live (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 民之所居). Zhu Xi: a neighbourhood with humane and generous ways is the fine one; to choose where to live and not settle in such a place is to lose the heart that tells right from wrong, and that cannot count as wisdom. 處 is chǔ, 'to dwell, to settle in' (Zhu Xi: 上聲); 焉 is yān, 'how?'; 知 is zhì, 'wise', the word later written 智 (Zhu Xi: 知去聲), and He Yan's text writes it 智. Mencius quotes the saying when he speaks of choosing a trade, and calls humaneness 'man's peaceful dwelling', so 里 can also be taken as a verb: 'to dwell in humaneness is the fine thing'. Variant: He Yan's text, as transcribed, has 善 'good' for 美 'beautiful'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不仁者，
不可以久處約，
不可以長處樂。
仁者安仁，
知者利仁。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Those who are not humane
cannot abide long in hardship,
cannot abide long in comfort.
The humane are at rest in humaneness;
the wise find their gain in humaneness.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man without humaneness cannot bear hardship for long, nor comfort for long either. The humane man is at rest in humaneness; the wise man holds to it because he sees the good of it.”
sentences.n: 約 is poverty and straits (Zhu Xi: 窮困也); 樂 is lè, 'ease, pleasure' (Zhu Xi: 音洛), not yuè 'music'; 長 is cháng, 'long'. 可以 is 'can', with 以 'thereby' hardly felt. Zhu Xi: the man without humaneness has lost his own heart — long in straits he goes to excess, long in pleasure he sinks into indulgence. 知 is zhì 'wise' again (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 利 Zhu Xi glosses 貪 'to covet': the wise know humaneness deeply and love it hard, so they are bent on having it (so it is not 'profit' in a base sense); He Yan's Wang Su says the wise know humaneness is fine and so find it profitable to practise. Zhu Xi: the humane rest in it and are never otherwise; the wise profit by it and do not change what they hold; the depth differs, but nothing outside can take it from either. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: resting in humaneness is one, profiting by it is two.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
惟仁者，
能好人，
能惡人。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Only the humane
can love people,
can hate people.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Only the humane man is able to love people as they should be loved, and hate them as they should be hated.”
sentences.n: 惟 wéi is 'only' (Zhu Xi: 惟之為言獨也). 好 hào and 惡 wù are the verbs 'to love' and 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 好惡皆去聲), not hǎo 'good' and è 'bad'. Zhu Xi: having no selfish heart, the humane like and dislike just as principle requires — what Master Cheng called 'getting it fair and right'. He quotes You Zuo: loving the good and hating the bad is a feeling everyone shares, yet people miss the mark, because their heart is tied to something and they cannot master themselves; the humane have no selfish heart, and so can love and hate. He Yan's Kong Anguo: only the humane can judge what is to be loved and hated in people.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
茍志於仁矣，
無惡也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Truly set on humaneness,
there is no evil.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If your heart is truly set on humaneness, you will do nothing evil.”
sentences.n: The edition prints 茍, a common old printed form of 苟 gǒu; Zhu Xi's comment on this line writes 苟 when it quotes Yang Shi, and both witnesses have 苟. Zhu Xi, like He Yan's Kong Anguo, glosses it 誠 'truly' rather than 'if'. 志 is to set the heart on, as in 2.4 志于學. 惡 here is è, 'evil, wrongdoing' (Zhu Xi: 惡如字), not wù 'to hate'. Zhu Xi: if the heart is truly in humaneness, there will be no doing of evil. He quotes Yang Shi: one set on humaneness may still act amiss, but he will not do evil. Variant: He Yan's text lacks the final 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
富與貴，
是人之所欲也；
不以其道得之，
不處也。
貧與賤，
是人之所惡也；
不以其道得之，
不去也。
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Wealth and rank —
these are what people desire;
not got by their proper way,
he does not abide in them.
Poverty and low station —
these are what people hate;
not got by their proper way,
he does not leave them.
sentences.i: The Master said: “Wealth and rank are what everyone wants; but if they came to him in the wrong way, he would not stay in them. Poverty and low station are what everyone hates; but even if they came to him undeserved, he would not run from them.
sentences.n: 與 is yǔ, 'and'; 惡 is wù, 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 所 makes the verb after it a noun: 所欲 'what they desire', 所惡 'what they hate'. 其道 'their way' is the proper road to them. Zhu Xi: 'not by their way' means getting what one ought not to get; then he will not stay in wealth and rank, and will not leave poverty and low station — so carefully does the gentleman weigh wealth and rank, and so calmly does he accept poverty. The second 不以其道得之 sits oddly (who comes to poverty 'by its proper way'?), and Zhu Xi reads it as the first: a poverty he did not deserve. He Yan's commentary says the same in its own way: the times have good fortune and bad, and a gentleman who walks the Way may still fall into poverty; this is getting it 'not by its way', and though men hate it he may not run from it. Who 'he' is comes in the next line: the gentleman. Variant: He Yan's text lacks 也 after 所惡 and after 不去.

sentences.t:
君子去仁，
惡乎成名？

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The gentleman, leaving humaneness —
by what would he make good his name?
sentences.i: A gentleman who abandons humaneness — what is left to make him worthy of the name?
sentences.n: 惡 here is wū (Zhu Xi: 平聲), a question word, 'where? how?'; 惡乎 is 'in what? by what?'. 成名 is not 'to become famous' but 'to make good the name' — the name of gentleman. Zhu Xi: a gentleman is a gentleman by his humaneness; if he covets wealth and rank and shrinks from poverty, he has left his own humaneness and has none of the substance of a gentleman — how would he make good the name? He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it the same: he cannot make good the name of gentleman.

sentences.t:
君子無終食之閒違仁；
造次必於是，
顛沛必於是。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The gentleman does not part from humaneness even while a single meal is eaten. Hurried and pressed, he is still in it; thrown down and in turmoil, he is still in it.”
sentences.n: 終食之閒 'the space of finishing a meal' — Zhu Xi: the time of one meal. 閒 is the edition's form of 間 jiān, 'interval'. 造次 is a bound word, 'in haste, at a pinch' (Zhu Xi: 急遽苟且之時, moments of hurry when one makes do; He Yan's Ma Rong: 急遽); 顛沛 is 'toppling and falling' (Zhu Xi: 傾覆流離之際, times of collapse and being cast adrift; Ma Rong: 僵仆, falling flat). 是 'this' is humaneness. Zhu Xi reads 造 as cào (七到反); modern practice says zào, and we give that. 沛 is pèi (Zhu Xi: 音貝). Zhu Xi: from the choice between wealth and poverty to the space of a meal, a moment of hurry, a time of ruin, there is no time and no place where the gentleman does not put his strength into humaneness; and when the choosing is clear the keeping is close, and the closer the keeping, the clearer the choosing.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
我未見好仁者，
惡不仁者。
好仁者，
無以尚之；
惡不仁者，
其為仁矣，
不使不仁者加乎其身。
sentences.l:
The Master said: “I have not yet seen one who loves humaneness,
one who hates the inhumane.
One who loves humaneness
has nothing to put above it;
one who hates the inhumane,
in practising humaneness,
lets nothing inhumane be laid upon his person.
sentences.i: The Master said: “I have never yet seen a man who truly loves humaneness, or one who truly hates what is inhumane. A man who loved it would set nothing higher. A man who hated its opposite would practise humaneness so that nothing inhumane could touch him.
sentences.n: 好 hào and 惡 wù again (Zhu Xi: 皆去聲). 不仁者 here is 'what is not humane' as much as 'those who are not'. 無以尚之 'has nothing with which to top it'. 其為仁矣 'as for his practising humaneness'; 為 is wéi. 乎 here is 'upon', standing for 於. Zhu Xi: one who loves humaneness truly knows it is lovable, so nothing in the world can be put above it; one who hates the inhumane truly knows it is hateful, so in practising humaneness he cuts away every inhumane thing and lets not the least of it come near him. Both are the deeds of complete virtue, which is why they are hard to find. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 無以尚之 as 'he cannot be surpassed', and ranks the lover of humaneness above the hater of the inhumane.

sentences.t:
有能一日用其力於仁矣乎？
我未見力不足者。
sentences.l:
Is there one who can, for a single day, spend his strength on humaneness?
I have not yet seen one whose strength was not enough.
sentences.i: Is there anyone able, for one single day, to put his whole strength into humaneness? I have never seen anyone whose strength fell short.
sentences.n: 矣乎 together ask 'has it ever come about that…?'. Zhu Xi: though men who love and hate in this way are not to be seen, if someone did, for one day, rouse himself to put his strength into humaneness, I have not seen that his strength would fail; for humaneness lies in oneself — want it, and it is there — and where the will goes, the energy follows. So humaneness is hard to perfect, but easy to come to. He Yan's Kong Anguo: no one manages to use his strength on humaneness for a single day, yet I have never seen anyone who wanted to be humane and lacked the strength. Variant: He Yan's text adds 也 after 力不足者.

sentences.t:
蓋有之矣，
我未之見也。」
sentences.l:
Perhaps there are such;
I have not yet seen them.”
sentences.i: Perhaps there are such men, but I have not met one.”
sentences.n: 蓋 is 'perhaps', a word of doubt (Zhu Xi: 疑辭). 未之見 'not yet them seen': after a negative, a pronoun object comes before the verb (未見之 → 未之見). Zhu Xi takes 有之 to mean men who do put out their strength and find it not enough — so dull and weak that they want to go forward and cannot; the Master, not wanting to end by calling humaneness easy, allows that there may be such, and sighs that no one is willing to try. Variant: He Yan's text reads 蓋有之乎 'perhaps there are?'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人之過也，
各於其黨。
觀過，
斯知仁矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “People's faults —
each goes by his kind.
Look at the faults,
and then one knows humaneness.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man's faults are of a piece with the kind of man he is. Look at his faults, and you can tell whether he is humane.”
sentences.n: 黨 is 'kind, class' here (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 類也), not 'faction'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: men's faults go by their kind — the gentleman errs on the side of generosity, the small man on the side of meanness; the gentleman errs in loving too much, the small man in being too hard. He quotes Yin Tun: from this one can know whether a man is humane; and in his own remark adds that this does not mean we must wait for a man to err before judging him, only that even his faults show how generous or mean he is. Kong Anguo reads it otherwise: a small man cannot act as a gentleman does, and this is no fault of his; he should be forgiven, not blamed — to look at faults and put the worthy and the foolish each in their place is humaneness. Variant: our first collation witness reads 斯知人矣 'then one knows the man'; He Yan's text has 民之過 'the people's faults'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
朝聞道，
夕死可矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “In the morning, to hear the Way;
in the evening, to die — that would do.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hear the Way at dawn, and death at nightfall would leave nothing to grieve over.”
sentences.n: 朝 is zhāo, 'morning' (not cháo 'court'). 可 'it is acceptable, it will do'. Zhu Xi glosses 道 here as 'the principle of how things ought to be' (事物當然之理): if one does get to hear it, then living one goes along with it and dying one is at peace, with nothing left undone to grieve over; 'morning' and 'evening' stress how short the time is. He quotes Master Cheng: a man cannot not know the Way; if he does get to hear it, even dying is acceptable — and since life and death are great matters, unless one had really gained something, how could one call dying that evening acceptable? He Yan's comment reads it as a lament: the Master was coming near death without hearing that the Way prevailed in the world.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
士志於道，
而恥惡衣惡食者，
未足與議也。」

morph.gloss: an officer, a man of service

sentences.l:
The Master said: “An officer set on the Way
who is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food
is not yet worth discussing it with.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man whose heart is set on the Way, yet is ashamed of shabby clothes and plain fare, is not someone to talk the Way over with.”
sentences.n: 士 is the class of men who serve as officers, and in the Analects a man who aspires to learning and office. 惡 here is è, 'bad, poor', an adjective. 與議 'to discuss with (him)'; 與 is yǔ. Zhu Xi: his heart wants the Way, yet he is ashamed that his mouth and body are not as well served as other men's — his understanding is low and mean indeed; how is he worth discussing the Way with? He quotes Master Cheng: set on the Way, yet with his heart in the service of outside things — how could he be worth discussing it with?

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子之於天下也，
無適也，無莫也，
義之與比。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman, toward all the world,
has nothing he singles out,
nothing he refuses:
what is right — with that he keeps.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “In the affairs of the world the gentleman has nothing he insists on and nothing he refuses out of hand. Whatever is right, he goes along with that.”
sentences.n: 適 is read dí (Zhu Xi: 丁歷反) and means 'to be singly set on' (Zhu Xi: 專主, citing the Zuo tradition's 吾誰適從 'whom shall I single out to follow?'); 莫 is 'to be unwilling' (Zhu Xi: 不肯). 之 after 君子 joins subject and phrase: 'the gentleman, in relation to the world'. 義之與比 puts the object first, marked by 之: 'what is right, with it he keeps'; 比 is bì, 'to follow, keep close to' (Zhu Xi: 必二反…從也). Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: 適 is 'it will do' and 莫 'it will not'; to have neither, with no Way to steer by, comes close to running wild — this is how the Buddhists and Daoists, saying the mind dwells nowhere, came to offend against the sages; the sage's learning is otherwise: between 'it will do' and 'it will not', what is right is there. He Yan's comment: the gentleman has nothing in the world he covets or longs for, and goes only where right is. Variant: He Yan's text ends 義之與比也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子懷德，
小人懷土；
君子懷刑，
小人懷惠。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman keeps virtue in mind,
the small man his land;
the gentleman keeps the law in mind,
the small man favours.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman's thoughts turn to virtue, the small man's to his plot of land; the gentleman's to the law and its penalties, the small man's to what he can get from others.”
sentences.n: 懷 Zhu Xi glosses 思念 'to think of, keep in mind'. Zhu Xi: 懷德 is holding on to the good one has by nature; 懷土 is being sunk in the comfort of where one lives; 懷刑 is fearing the law; 懷惠 is coveting gain — the gentleman and the small man face different ways, as the public and the private differ. He quotes Yin Tun: to delight in good and hate what is not good makes a gentleman; to seek ease and grab what one can makes a small man. 刑 is punishment, and the law that threatens it. He Yan's Kong Anguo glosses 懷 as 安 'to be at ease in': the gentleman is at ease in virtue and in the law; the small man is loath to move from his land; and Bao Xian takes 惠 as favours bestowed.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
放於利而行，
多怨。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Going by profit in acting —
much resentment.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Act with an eye only to profit, and you will earn much resentment.”
sentences.n: 放 here is fǎng (Zhu Xi: 上聲), 'to rely on, go by' (Kong Anguo, whom Zhu Xi quotes: 依也), not fàng 'to let go'. 行 is xíng, 'to act'. 多怨 Kong Anguo explains as 'to draw much resentment' on oneself. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: whoever wants profit for himself is bound to harm others, and so draws much resentment.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
能以禮讓為國乎，
何有？
不能以禮讓為國，
如禮何？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Can one govern a state with the rites and yielding?
Then what is there to it?
If one cannot govern a state with the rites and yielding,
what of the rites?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a ruler can govern his state by the rites and the yielding that is their substance, what difficulty will he have? If he cannot govern it that way, the rites can do nothing for him.”
sentences.n: 讓 is yielding, giving place to others; Zhu Xi calls it 'the substance of the rites' (禮之實). 為國 is 'to run a state'; 為 is wéi. 何有 'what is there (to it)?' means it is no difficulty (Zhu Xi and He Yan both: 言不難也). 如禮何 'what about the rites?', as in 3.3. Zhu Xi: with the substance of the rites one governs a state with ease; without it, the forms of the rites, however complete, can do nothing — let alone govern a state. He Yan's Bao Xian: 'what of the rites?' means he cannot use the rites. Variant: our first collation witness has 能以禮讓為國，於從政乎何有 'what difficulty would he have in government?', the wording of 6.6; Zhu Xi's and He Yan's texts lack 於從政.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不患無位，
患所以立。
不患莫己知，
求為可知也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Don't be troubled at having no office; be troubled about whether you have what it takes to fill one. Don't be troubled that no one recognises you; work at having something in you that deserves to be recognised.”
sentences.n: The print has 已, a misprint for 己, corrected here. (The Siku copy confuses 己, 已 and 巳 throughout; the Master Cheng saying Zhu Xi quotes on this line has 求其在己者, and our first collation witness reads 己.) 莫己知 is 'no one knows me': after a negative such as 莫 'no one', a pronoun object comes before the verb (己知 for 知己), as in 1.16 不患人之不己知. 位 is an official post; 所以立 is 'that by which (one would) stand' in it (Zhu Xi: 所以立乎其位者). 可知 'can be known' — Zhu Xi: the substance that would get one known. He quotes Master Cheng: the gentleman seeks what lies in himself, and that is all. He Yan's Bao Xian: seek the good Way and learn to practise it, and others will know you. Variant: He Yan's text adds 也 after the first 知.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
參乎！
吾道一以貫之。」
曾子曰：「唯。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Shen!
My Way — one thing strings it through.”
Master Zeng said: “Yes.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Shen! There is one thing that runs through the whole of my Way.” “Yes,” said Master Zeng.
sentences.n: 參 is Master Zeng's personal name, read shēn (Zhu Xi: 所金反); the Master calls him by it, as a teacher calls a pupil. 貫 is 'to string together, run through' (Zhu Xi: 通也); 一以貫之 is 'with one thing, string it through'. 唯 is wěi (Zhu Xi: 上聲), the prompt 'yes' of a son or pupil answering at once — Zhu Xi: an answer quick and without doubt; He Yan's Kong Anguo: he understood straight away and did not ask, so he answered 'yes'. Zhu Xi: the sage's heart is one undivided principle, answering everything everywhere, each use different; Master Zeng had already examined and practised each of its uses, but did not yet know that they were one in substance; the Master saw he was near to it, called him and told him, and Master Zeng grasped the point in silence. Variant: He Yan's text reads 一以貫之哉.

sentences.t:
子出。
門人問曰：「何謂也？」
曾子曰：「
夫子之道，
忠恕
而已矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master went out. The disciples asked, saying: “What did he mean?”
Master Zeng said: “The Master's Way
is wholeheartedness and fellow-feeling,
and that is all.”
sentences.i: When the Master had gone out, the disciples asked: “What did he mean?” Master Zeng said: “The Master's Way is to be wholehearted, and to put yourself in the other man's place — that and nothing else.”
sentences.n: 門人 'the men of the gate' are the disciples. 忠 is our 'wholehearted(ness)'; 恕 'fellow-feeling'. Zhu Xi defines the pair: 'to give all of oneself is 忠, to extend oneself (to others) is 恕' (盡己之謂忠，推己之謂恕), and he records the gloss read from the shapes of the characters: 中心 'the heart at the centre' makes 忠, 如心 'a heart like (another's)' makes 恕. 而已矣 'and that is all' — Zhu Xi: it marks something exhausted, with nothing left over. Zhu Xi: the Master's one principle answers everything as the perfect sincerity of Heaven and Earth gives each thing its place; Master Zeng saw this but found it hard to put into words, so he borrowed the learner's terms, giving all of oneself and extending oneself, to make it plain. He quotes Master Cheng: 忠 is the Way of Heaven and 恕 the Way of man; 忠 is the substance and 恕 its use.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子喻於義；
小人喻於利。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is versed in what is right;
the small man is versed in profit.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What the gentleman knows through and through is what is right; what the small man knows through and through is profit.”
sentences.n: 喻 is 'to see clearly, understand' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 猶曉也). Zhu Xi: 義 is what Heaven's principle makes fitting, 利 what human feeling desires. He quotes Master Cheng: the gentleman is to what is right as the small man is to profit — each knows his own thing deeply, and so loves it deeply; and Yang Shi: some gentlemen give up their lives to take what is right; reckoned by profit, men want nothing more than life and hate nothing more than death, so who would give up life for right? What such a man understands is right alone; he does not know profit as profit. The small man is the reverse.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
見賢思齊焉；
見不賢而内自省也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Seeing worth, think of being level with it;
seeing the unworthy, search within yourself.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When you see a man of worth, think how you might come up to him; when you see a man without worth, turn and search your own conduct.”
sentences.n: 齊 is qí, 'to be level with, equal'; 焉 'with him'. 省 is xǐng, 'to examine' (Zhu Xi: 悉井反), as in 1.4 吾日三省吾身. 内 is the edition's form of 內. Zhu Xi: one hopes to have the same good, and fears to have the same bad. He quotes Hu Yin: whoever sees good and bad in others and always turns back on himself will neither envy others idly while giving himself up, nor blame others and forget to blame himself. He Yan's Bao Xian: to think of being the equal of the worthy man. Variant: He Yan's text reads 見不賢者 'seeing one who is not worthy'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
事父母，
㡬諫；
見志不從，
又敬，不違；
勞而不怨。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “In serving your parents, if you must point out their faults, do it gently. If you see they are not minded to listen, go on being respectful and do not defy them; and if it brings hardship on you, bear them no grudge.”
sentences.n: 㡬 is the edition's form of 幾 jī, 'slight, subtle' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Bao Xian: 微也) — 'gently, by hints'. 諫 is to remonstrate, to point out a superior's fault. Zhu Xi reads the passage with the 'Domestic Rules' (內則) chapter of the Record of Rites: when parents err, the son remonstrates with lowered breath, a pleasant face and a soft voice; if they do not take it, he grows more reverent and more filial, and when they are pleased he remonstrates again; rather than let them offend the village and the neighbourhood he presses them earnestly, and if they are angry and beat him till the blood runs, he does not dare to resent it, but grows more reverent and filial. On that reading 不違 is 'do not go against them', though he keeps at the matter, and 勞 is the hardship he suffers. He Yan's Bao Xian takes 不違 as 'not daring to go against his parents' wishes by pressing his remonstrance'. Variant: He Yan's text lacks 而 in 勞而不怨.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
父母在，
不遠遊；
遊必有方。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “While father and mother live, do not travel far;
if you travel, there must be a set place.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “While your parents are alive, do not go on long journeys; and if you do go, keep to the place you said you were going.”
sentences.n: 在 is 'to be present, to be alive', as in 1.11 父在. 方 is a direction, a quarter: a known destination (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 方猶常也, 'a fixed place'). Zhu Xi: travelling far takes a son a long way from his parents for many days, the morning and evening attendance lapses and news grows scarce; not only can he not stop thinking of them, he fears they cannot stop thinking of him. 'There must be a set place': if he has said he is going east, he does not then go west, so that his parents always know where he is and do not worry, and if they send for him he will surely come. He quotes Fan Zuyu: a son who can take his parents' heart as his own heart is filial. Variant: He Yan's text reads 父母在，子不遠遊 'the son does not travel far'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
三年無改於父之道，
可謂孝矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Three years without changing from his father's way —
he can be called filial.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If for three years he makes no change to his father's ways, he may be called a good son.”
sentences.n: These words repeat the second half of 1.11, and the English is the same. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: it has already appeared in the first book; here it probably occurs again and has lost its first half. 三年 is the mourning period for a parent. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: a filial son in mourning, grieving and longing, makes no change to his father's way, because his heart could not bear to.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
父母之年，
不可不知也。
一則以喜，
一則以懼。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Father's and mother's years
must not go unknown:
on the one side, for gladness;
on the other, for fear.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Keep your parents' ages always in mind — glad that they have lived so long, afraid that they are growing old.”
sentences.n: 不可不 'cannot not' is a strong 'must'. 知 here Zhu Xi glosses 記憶 'to keep in memory'. 一則…一則… is 'on the one hand…, on the other…'; 以 'thereby, for'. Zhu Xi: if one always knows one's parents' age, one is both glad of their long life and afraid of their decline, and from this comes, of itself, the wish to make the most of every day with them. He Yan's Kong Anguo: seeing them live long, one is glad; seeing them grow frail, afraid.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
古者言之不出，
恥躬之不逮也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The men of old not letting their words out
was shame at their persons not reaching them.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The men of old kept their words in, for fear of the shame of not living up to them.”
sentences.n: 古者 is 'in antiquity' or 'the men of old'. 之 between subject and verb turns 言不出 and 躬不逮 into noun phrases: 'words not coming out', 'the person not reaching'. 躬 is one's own person, one's conduct; 逮 is 'to reach, come up to' (Zhu Xi: 及也). Zhu Xi: speaking of the men of old shows that the present is otherwise; for conduct to fall short of words is the deepest shame, and that is why the men of old did not let their words out. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the gentleman speaks only when he cannot help it — not because speaking is hard, but because doing is; it is because men do not act that they speak lightly; if one spoke only as one acted, and acted as one spoke, words would not come easily out of one's mouth. Variant: He Yan's text reads 言之不出也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
以約失之者，
鮮矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Those who go wrong through restraint
are few.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Few people go astray by holding themselves in.”
sentences.n: 約 here is 'to hold in, restrain' — Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: not to be lavish and let oneself go is called 約; and Yin Tun: whatever one does, with restraint one seldom goes wrong — it does not mean frugality only. 鮮 is xiǎn, 'few' (Zhu Xi: 上聲), as in 1.2 and 1.3. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 約 as frugality: neither lavishness nor thrift hits the mean, but lavishness breeds arrogance and calls down disaster, while thrift brings no trouble.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子欲訥於言，
而敏於行。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman wants to be slow in speech
and quick in action.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman would rather his words come slowly and his deeds quickly.”
sentences.n: 訥 is slow of speech, words coming with difficulty (He Yan's Bao Xian: 遲鈍 'slow and dull'). 敏 'quick, diligent', as in 1.14 敏於事而慎於言. Zhu Xi marks 行 as 去聲, the old tone for 'conduct'; modern practice does not keep it, and we give xíng (see 1.11). Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: letting words out is easy, so one wants to be slow; doing with all one's strength is hard, so one wants to be quick. He also quotes Hu Yin: the ten passages from 'my Way, one thing strings it through' (4.15) to here were probably all recorded by Master Zeng's disciples.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
德不孤，
必有鄰。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Virtue is not alone;
it surely has neighbours.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Virtue is never left without company: its own kind will settle round it, as neighbours do.”
sentences.n: 孤 is 'orphaned, alone'. 鄰 is a neighbour; Zhu Xi glosses it 親 'those close to one'. Zhu Xi: virtue does not stand by itself; its own kind answers it, so whoever has virtue is sure to have others of his kind follow him, as a man who settles somewhere has neighbours. He Yan's comment: things gather by kind, and those with the same aims seek each other out; so virtue must have neighbours, and is not alone.

sentences.t:
子游曰：「
事君，數斯辱矣；
朋友數斯疏矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)

sentences.l:
Ziyou said: “Serving a lord, keep at him over and over, and then comes disgrace;
with friends, keep at them over and over, and then comes distance.”
sentences.i: Ziyou said: “Press your advice on your lord time and again and you will be disgraced; press it on your friends time and again and they will keep away from you.”
sentences.n: 子游 Ziyou is the disciple Yan Yan 言偃 (see 2.7). 數 is read shuò, 'frequent, too often' (Zhu Xi: 色角反; he quotes Master Cheng: 煩數 'tiresomely often'). 斯 'then'. 疏 is 'distant, estranged'. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: when remonstrance with a lord is not acted on, one should leave; when a friend will not take good advice, one should stop; to keep pressing makes the speaker cheap and the hearer weary, so one seeks honour and gets disgrace, seeks closeness and gets distance. And Fan Zuyu: lord and minister, friend and friend are both joined by what is right, so the two cases are the same. He Yan's comment reads 數 as 'hasty, pressing'. Book 4 ends here, and so does the second juan of Zhu Xi's commentary.
